\chapter{Right and Left}
\label{ch:mr-right-and-left}
\hlchaptermodality{44}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the right and left sides with an adjective that agrees with its noun, and I can run every place word in the book off one bent stem.}

Complete MR-R44-directions and bend ghar once, then run madhye, var, khālī, javaḷ and samor off that single stem before adding a side with ujvā or ḍāvā.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ujvā]{\mr{उजवा} (ujvā) — right}

\label{lesson:MR-C44-ujva}



\begin{quote}
A direction needs a side, and \emph{in front of} is only one of them.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{lāmb}, then \emph{samor}, and put a room in front of a house
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{उजवा}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{उजवा}} — \emph{ujvā} — \textbf{right (the side)}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{उजवा} \mr{डोळा}} — \emph{ujvā ḍoḷā} — \textbf{the right eye}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{उजवा}} is an adjective, so it comes BEFORE its noun and it agrees with it: \textbf{\mr{उजवा}} with a masculine noun, \textbf{\mr{उजवी}} with a feminine, \textbf{\mr{उजवं}} with a neuter. You have seen that three-way ending before, on \textbf{\mr{माझा} / \mr{माझी} / \mr{माझं}}, and it is the same three endings doing the same job.

Its history is a good one to keep. The Sanskrit word \emph{ṛju} meant \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{straight, upright},\textquotedblright{} and the right hand was the straight one — the hand that does the proper thing. The very same idea sits inside Latin \emph{rectus} and therefore inside English \textbf{right}, which is both a side and a correctness. Two languages made the same joke independently, out of the same root.

To send somebody rightwards you add the \textbf{-\mr{कडे}} you will meet later, giving \textbf{\mr{उजवीकडे}}. For now, the side itself is enough.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ujvā} — right
  \item \emph{ujvā ḍoḷā} — the right eye
  \item \emph{ujvī khoolī} — and hear the ending follow the noun
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \textbf{\mr{उजवा}} stand relative to its noun? (\textbf{Before it}.) What did its Sanskrit ancestor mean? (\emph{\textbf{Straight}} — the same idea as English \emph{right}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%89\%E0\%A4\%9C\%E0\%A4\%B5\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{उजवा}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ḍāvā]{\mr{डावा} (ḍāvā) — left}

\label{lesson:MR-C44-daava}



\begin{quote}
One side is not a pair. Say \textbf{\mr{उजवा}} once and then take the other hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{डावा}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{डावा}} — \emph{ḍāvā} — \textbf{left (the side)}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{डावा} \mr{कान}} — \emph{ḍāvā kān} — \textbf{the left ear}
\end{quote}

Everything you learned one lesson ago transfers whole: \textbf{\mr{डावा}} is an adjective, it stands before its noun, and it agrees — \textbf{\mr{डावा}}, \textbf{\mr{डावी}}, \textbf{\mr{डावं}}. Learning a pair of opposites together is cheaper than learning two words, because the second one costs only its sound.

It opens with \textbf{\mr{ड}}, the retroflex \emph{d}, so the tongue curls back the way it does in \textbf{\mr{डोळा}}. Keep it apart from the dental \textbf{\mr{द}} of \textbf{\mr{दूध}}: the two sound close to an English ear and Marathi treats them as different letters entirely.

Now you can take somebody through a door: \textbf{\mr{उजवा}} or \textbf{\mr{डावा}}, then a landmark with \textbf{\mr{समोर}} or \textbf{\mr{जवळ}}, and the direction is complete.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ḍāvā} — left, with the tongue curled on the \textbf{\mr{ड}}
  \item \emph{ḍāvā kān}, then \emph{ujvā kān}
  \item \emph{ḍāvī khoolī} — and hear the feminine ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter does \textbf{\mr{डावा}} start with, and which taught word shares it? (\textbf{\mr{ड}}, as in \textbf{\mr{डोळा}}.) How much of \textbf{\mr{उजवा}}'s grammar did \textbf{\mr{डावा}} need you to learn again? (\textbf{None of it}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A1\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%B5\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{डावा}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ujvā · ḍāvā]{Say where something is, five ways, from one stem}

\label{lesson:MR-R44-directions}



\begin{quote}
Four chapters ago the only answer you had to \textbf{\mr{कुठे}?} was a pointed finger. Name every answer you have now.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gharā-} once, then run \emph{madhye · var · khālī · javaḷ · samor}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{lāmb} — and notice it took no stem
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ujvā ḍoḷā}, \emph{ḍāvā kān} — the two sides, before their nouns
  \item \emph{Recall:} answer \emph{kuṭhe?} with \emph{ithe}, then \emph{tithe}, and write \textbf{\mr{तिथे}} once
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do five of this tranche's words demand of the noun in front of them, and which two do not? (\textbf{The oblique stem}; \textbf{\mr{लांब}}, \textbf{\mr{उजवा}} and \textbf{\mr{डावा}} are not postpositions.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
